title: Computation graphs and the chain rule
description: Lecture graph forward and backward, then a branching-path extension.
source_short: Lecture 2 / PDF p.27 / branching extension explicitly labelled
source: Lecture 2 - Logistic Regression + Neural Network.pdf, page 27; branching example is an original extension.

pages.title: Break one expression into small steps
pages.subtitle: Lecture 2, page 27: a computation graph records which values depend on which.
blocks: Arrows show the forward flow of values. u and v are intermediate results. We compute values forward and sensitivities backward.

pages.title: Forward pass: save every node value
pages.subtitle: Compute a node only after its inputs are known.
blocks: Saving u and v avoids repeatedly expanding the full expression. Saving b and c matters because the backward calculation needs their values.
A node value answers "what number did we compute?" A derivative answers "how sensitive is the final result to a small change?"

pages.title: Local derivatives: inspect one operation
pages.subtitle: Hold the other inputs fixed when differentiating an operation.
blocks: An addition node passes sensitivity to each input unchanged: multiply by 1.
A multiplication node uses the OTHER input as its local derivative. Changing b affects u in proportion to c.

pages.title: Backward pass: multiply along each path
pages.subtitle: The chain rule multiplies upstream sensitivity by the next local derivative.

blocks.eq: \frac{\partial J}{\partial u}=\frac{\partial J}{\partial v}\frac{\partial v}{\partial u}=3(1)=3
\frac{\partial J}{\partial a}=\frac{\partial J}{\partial v}\frac{\partial v}{\partial a}=3(1)=3
\frac{\partial J}{\partial b}=\frac{\partial J}{\partial u}\frac{\partial u}{\partial b}=3(2)=6
\frac{\partial J}{\partial c}=\frac{\partial J}{\partial u}\frac{\partial u}{\partial c}=3(3)=9

blocks: Near these inputs, increasing b by 0.01 increases J by about 6 times 0.01 = 0.06. The derivative and the node value u both happen to equal 6 here; they mean different things.

pages.title: A shared input can affect two paths
pages.subtitle: Original study extension: add b squared to the lecture expression.
blocks: b now influences F through u and through q. Both effects matter. F and q are new extension nodes, not nodes from the lecture slide.

pages.title: At a branch, add the path contributions
pages.subtitle: Changing b changes both J and q, so their effects on F add.

blocks.eq: \frac{\partial F}{\partial b}=\frac{\partial F}{\partial J}\frac{\partial J}{\partial b}+\frac{\partial F}{\partial q}\frac{\partial q}{\partial b}

blocks: Multiply derivatives ALONG a path; add contributions FROM different paths. Do not discard one branch or multiply the two branch contributions.
We have computed sensitivities only. A parameter update would be a separate step using a learning rate.

pages.title: Your turn: include a negative input
pages.subtitle: Use the lecture graph first, then add the branching extension.
blocks: 1. Calculate u = bc, v = a + u, and J = 3v.
2. Calculate the three derivatives of J with respect to a, b and c.
3. Add q = b squared and F = J + q. Calculate F and its derivative with respect to b.
Show each local derivative and each path contribution, not just the final answers.

pages.title: Practice answer: follow values and paths
pages.subtitle: The negative c makes the J path contribution for b negative.
blocks: The branches partly cancel. Common mistakes: using b instead of c for the derivative of bc with respect to b, or confusing F = 1 with its derivative also being 1 here.
